tier_reason: Independent third-party measurement: the Lingua README 'How fast is it?' table (Whichlang 4.47 ms vs CLD 2 23.92 ms single thread, 651.89 us vs 4.81 ms multi thread) was produced by the Lingua author, not the Whichlang or CLD2 authors, with a public Criterion harness (benches/benchmark.rs) on a stated iMac 3.6 GHz 8-core Core i9. Not A because neither the rustc version nor the C++ compiler used for CLD2 is stated and the CPU is described rather than named; upgraded from C on the independence of the measurement.

corrections.baseline: CLD2 (Google Compact Language Detector 2, C++), called through the deprecated cld2 1.0.2 crate (emk/rust-cld2), whose cld2-sys build.rs compiles the bundled CLD2 sources plus a thin C++ wrapper with the gcc crate and -std=c++03; the Rust side calls CLD2_ExtDetectLanguageSummary4 over FFI. Whatlang (Rust) and Lingua (Rust) are also compared.
corrections.workload: Lingua benches/benchmark.rs (Criterion): 16 sentences, one per language in the common 16-language set, repeated 125 times, giving 2,000 detections per iteration, single thread and rayon multi-thread. Second table: the accuracy_reports binary classifying 3,000 texts (1,000 single words, 1,000 word pairs, 1,000 sentences) for each of Lingua's 75 languages, timed together with statistics collection and report-file writing.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated on the page. 'cargo bench --features benchmark' implies the bench profile (rustc opt-level 3); the gcc crate used by cld2-sys passes cargo's OPT_LEVEL to the C++ compiler, so CLD2 was presumably built at -O3 with -std=c++03 (inferred from cld2-sys/build.rs, not stated). rustc and C++ compiler versions are not given.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Lingua README 'How fast is it?': Whichlang 4.47 ms vs CLD 2 23.92 ms single thread (about 5.4x, derived from page data) and 651.89 us vs 4.81 ms multi thread (about 7.4x, derived from page data); accuracy-reporter run time Whichlang 0.28 s vs CLD 2 1.70 s (about 6.1x, derived from page data; this row includes harness overhead, see caveats). Whichlang's own README compares only with Whatlang (about 10x faster; 0.26 us vs 16.62 us short text, 5.21 us vs 62.00 us long text) and claims above 100 MB/s (105.69 and 112.31 MiB/s).
corrections.why_faster: Different model and task scope, not Rust codegen. Whichlang scores hashed 2-4-gram letter and codepoint features with a 16-class multiclass logistic regression projected into a 4,096-dimension space (Whichlang README). CLD2 runs its quadgram scoring tables over its whole language set (the cld2 crate has no allowlist, so it is not restricted to the 16 common languages) and computes a top-3 summary with percentages and normalized scores through ExtDetectLanguageSummary4. The smaller model and the narrower language set are the likely reasons; no profile is published.
corrections.caveats: The CLD2 comparison is in a competitor's README (Lingua), not in Whichlang's own. The Criterion input is only 16 distinct sentences repeated 125 times (tiny, cache-resident working set). CLD2 considers all of its languages while Whichlang knows only 16, so the two do different amounts of work; the single-thread table is a Whichlang-versus-CLD2 library result, not a Rust-versus-C++ one (Whatlang, also Rust, is slower than CLD2 single-threaded at 36.24 ms). The 0.28 s vs 1.70 s accuracy-reporter row times statistics collection and report writing too, and Lingua's CLD2 adapter maps each result by iterating all Lingua languages and allocating an ISO-code String per candidate, which penalises the CLD2 row. CLD2 build flags (-O3) are inferred from the gcc crate, not stated; the cld2 binding crate is deprecated and bundles CLD2 sources from about 2015. Whichlang supports only 16 languages; Lingua reports it is less accurate than Lingua on that common set.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 461 stars; about 469,000 crates.io downloads (latest 0.1.1, 2025-01-21); used by Quickwit

notes: Numbers match the Lingua README exactly; the C++ baseline really is CLD2 compiled from source through the cld2 crate's FFI wrapper, presumably at -O3. Record as a Whichlang library win over CLD2 (different model, fewer languages), not a language-level win; harness shortcomings: 16 repeated sentences, CLD2 scores all its languages, and the accuracy-reporter timing includes report writing and an allocation-heavy CLD2 language mapping. Tier raised from C to B because the measurement is independent of both projects.

tier_reason: First-party README table only: no benchmark script in the repository (src holds only main.zig and scanner.zig), no CPU model, no versions or build flags for zog, jq, jaq or ripgrep, and jq and jaq share one column. The largest ratio (about 58x) exceeds 50x with flags unstated, so C is also the cap.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: '20-50x faster than jq/jaq for typical queries', '4.1x faster than ripgrep for complex multi-condition logic', aggregations '40x faster than jq'. Table, GB/s zog(file) / zog(pipe) / ripgrep / jq-jaq: simple key match 4.03 / 2.38 / 2.30 / 0.07; substring match (HAS) 2.49 / 2.09 / 1.53 / 0.07; numeric comparison 3.39 / 2.41 / 2.97 / 0.10; field extraction (TSV) 2.83 / 2.21 / N/A / 0.10; JSON re-formatting 2.77 / 2.18 / N/A / 0.10; aggregations 2.41 / 1.91 / N/A / 0.05; complex logic (OR/AND) 2.24 / 1.93 / 0.54 / 0.06. Ratios against jq/jaq: about 28-58x in file mode and 22-38x in pipe mode (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Build instructions say 'zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast' (build.zig falls back to Debug without the flag); the build mode, Zig version and flags of the benchmarked binary, and the versions and builds of jq, jaq and ripgrep, are not stated. The repo migrated from Zig 0.13.0 to 0.16.0 on 2026-07-02, so the README numbers may predate that.
corrections.workload: Search, filter, extract, re-format and aggregate over a 1 GB JSONL file with 6.7 million lines; GB/s per workload, zog reading a file (background reader thread with 8 MB double buffering) or a pipe. Whether the file was in the page cache, the dataset's shape and the exact queries and baseline command lines are not given.
corrections.caveats: First-party only: no CPU, no benchmark script or dataset in the repository, no baseline versions or flags, and jq and jaq are merged into one column. zog does different and weaker work than jq: it does not parse or validate JSON, ignores nesting (a key inside a sub-object matches as if it were a root key), matches numbers literally (90 does not equal 90.0) and assumes single-line UTF-8 JSONL, so its results can differ from jq's on the same query. zog(file) uses two threads (reader plus scanner) against single-threaded jq. ripgrep cannot express numeric comparisons natively, so its rows are some unstated regex approximation. A tool-versus-tool result, not a language comparison; arguably belongs in a JSON category as much as text.
corrections.why_faster: README 'Blind Scanner' architecture: no AST; 32-byte AVX2/NEON SIMD scanning with bitmasks and @ctz to find newlines and quoted keys; a background reader thread double-buffering 8 MB blocks; zero heap allocations during the scan; query pre-compiled into a plan (pre-quoted keys, pre-parsed numbers). jq builds a full value tree for every line. The win comes from skipping the parse and validation, not from Zig codegen.

notes: Numbers match the README; the record omitted the zog(pipe) column and the field-extraction and re-formatting rows, now added. Shortcomings to record: first-party, no script, CPU or baseline versions; jq/jaq merged column; zog trades correctness (nesting-blind, literal numeric matching, no validation) for speed, so it is not doing the same job as jq; tool-versus-tool, not a Zig-versus-C win.
